summary: Records the IETF's wishes about what rights the IETF Trust should grant to others for using IETF documents, including Internet-Drafts and RFCs. It is advice to the Trustees of the IETF Trust. This is an informational document, and it was replaced by RFC 8721.

eli5.summary: The IETF keeps a box of rules about who may copy and use its writings. This memo tells the people holding that box what the rules should say.

questions: what rights does the ietf trust grant for rfcs
can i use text from an rfc
can i extract code from an rfc
subtitle: Guiding principles for intellectual property rights in IETF documents.

tldr.problem: The IETF Trust holds intellectual property rights to IETF documents but needs clear direction on what rights to grant to the public for using those documents.
tldr.mechanism: This document articulates the IETF's wishes to the Trustees of the IETF Trust about what rights should be granted for copying, implementing, and using IETF Contributions.
tldr.outcome: The IETF Trust uses these wishes to craft licensing language that encourages interoperability while protecting authors' rights. This was superseded by RFC 8721.

today: RFC 5377 is obsoleted by RFC 8721, which provides the current IETF guidance on outbound rights in IETF documents.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The IETF Trust is an organization that holds the intellectual property rights for IETF documents, Internet-Drafts, and RFCs. These rights are granted to the Trust by contributors to the IETF. The Trustees of the IETF Trust are responsible for deciding what rights should be granted to the public when they use these documents.

This document represents the IETF's collective wishes about what those public rights ought to be. The Trustees will use this guidance to draft the actual legal language that appears in IETF documents, following the rules laid out in RFC 5378.
sections.eli5: The IETF Trust holds the copyright to internet standard documents. This memo tells them what permissions to give to people who want to use those documents.

sections.title: Purpose in Granting Rights
sections.content:
The IETF's mission is to produce documents that make the Internet work better. The most valuable IETF documents are those that specify protocols and standards, because implementors build systems using these specifications. The primary value comes from having many independent, interoperable implementations of the standard.

To encourage accurate and interoperable implementations, the IETF Trust grants copy rights to people so they can refer to and build from the RFC text. The same reasoning applies to Internet-Drafts, which early implementors use before final publication. Best Current Practice and Informational documents deserve similar treatment to encourage their widespread use.

Previous approaches included specific licensing text within RFCs themselves, but this proved problematic when legal issues needed correction. This document instead describes the IETF's intentions to the Trustees, leaving them to select and update the precise legal wording as needed.
sections.eli5: The IETF wants people to build lots of working systems from its standards. To do that, people need permission to read, reference, and build on the standard's descriptions. The Trust decides what permissions to give.

sections.title: Rights Granted for Different Uses
sections.content:
The IETF distinguishes between several categories of use, each with different recommended rights:

Full Reproduction: Anyone should be able to make complete copies of RFCs and translate them into other languages without modification. This enables wide dissemination and prevents loss of context.

Quotation: Excerpts of any length should be quotable in any context, with proper attribution to the IETF. Translations of quotations are also permitted. This supports teaching, research, and technical discussion.

Implementation from Code: IETF documents often include computer-processable components—ABNF definitions, XML schemas, MIBs, ASN.1, and code snippets. These are included for precision and clarity. Implementors should be able to extract these code components, modify them as needed, and use them in their products without restrictions, even in open-source projects with permissive licenses. The Trust should not add extra license obligations beyond those already in the contribution.

Text Reuse: As of this writing, there is no consensus to permit using text from RFCs in modified form. Individual authors may grant such rights separately from what the IETF grants.

Additional Licenses: Material in an IETF document may be available under other licenses. The IETF prefers to indicate this in the document rather than embed additional license text, to avoid any restriction on the rights the IETF grants.
sections.eli5: The rules are different for copying the whole thing, quoting a bit, using code snippets, or modifying the words. Code pieces should be easy to take and use anywhere. Text reuse is more restricted.

sections.title: Authority and Implementation
sections.content:
The legal authority for granting rights rests with the Trustees of the IETF Trust, who are the members of the IAOC (Internet Architecture Board). This document provides guidance based on rough consensus from the IETF. The Trustees have the responsibility and power to determine the exact text, mechanisms, and policies needed to meet these goals.

The Trustees are expected to begin drafting license text and materials immediately upon IESG approval of this document. Changes take effect as the Trustees determine. The Trustees cannot grant rights they do not receive from contributors, so they work within the constraints of what contributors provide. When possible, the Trust should retroactively offer similar rights for older RFCs, though this is not required to be a massive effort.

If contributors have concerns about the Trustees' actions, appeals are governed by BCP 101.
sections.eli5: The IETF Trust board is in charge of writing the actual rules. This memo tells them what the IETF thinks those rules should be. They can change the rules later if needed.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: RFC 5377 is an Informational document that articulates the IETF's position on intellectual property rights as of November 2008. It was later obsoleted by RFC 8721, which provides updated guidance on outbound rights for IETF documents.
sections.eli5: This memo says what the IETF wanted in 2008. A newer RFC (8721) updated the guidance later.
